3 Data and sample

Our sample includes firms that announced goodwill impairment losses during the
period 1996–2006, thus covering both SFAS 121 and SFAS 142 regulatory regimes.
We identify firms that announced goodwill impairment losses by searching the
Factiva database using ‘‘goodwill impairment,’’ ‘‘goodwill write off,’’ ‘‘SFAS 121,’’
‘‘SFAS 142,’’ and other variations of these key words. The transition provisions of
SFAS 142 relating to the impairment of existing goodwill are applicable in fiscal
years beginning after December 15, 2001. Hence, our search for transition losses
covers the period beginning December 15, 2001, and ending December 31, 2003,
which includes the first fiscal year of application of the standard for all companies.
Transition (after-tax) goodwill impairment loss is reported under ‘‘cumulative effect
of accounting change’’ as a below-the-line item in the income statement, while the
post-SFAS-142 loss (that is, nontransition impairment) is reported as an item of
operating income. <sup>4</sup> We only include the first announcement of a specific dollar
amount of impairment loss for a given quarter. <sup>5</sup> Announcements of a specific dollar

4 We verify the dollar amount of the goodwill impairment loss in the transition and post-SFAS-142
periods obtained from our Factiva search with the amount reported in Compustat; we use the amount
reported in the press release when it differs from that reported in Compustat. For the post-SFAS-142
period covering 2003 through 2006, the (after-tax) goodwill impairment loss is reported under data item
250.

5 We find considerable variation in the range of losses announced by companies, with a few narrow
ranges and a few ranges expressed from zero to millions of dollars. We exclude all announcements of
ranges because we believe that midpoints of wide ranges are not meaningful and imposing inclusion/
exclusion rules would be arbitrary.

From Table 1, Panel A, our final sample of 1,584 announcements of goodwill
impairment losses includes 477 announcements from the pre-SFAS-142 period (that
is, under SFAS 121), 253 from the transition period (that is, on adoption of SFAS
142), and 854 from the post-SFAS-142 period. From Panel B, a significantly higher
number of firms announce multiple goodwill write-offs in the post-SFAS-142 period
relative to the pre-SFAS-142 period (30% over the 5-year sample period vs. 12.5%
over the 6-year period).

Causes and consequences of goodwill impairment losses 753

Ramanna and Watts (2010) find that a significant number of firms with non-zero
goodwill and with potential goodwill impairment (as indicated by a market-to-book
ratio [1 in year t - 2 and \1 in years t - 1 and t) did not take write-offs under
SFAS 142. Their finding suggests that focusing solely on the sample of firms that
have selected to take impairment losses can potentially lead to biased inferences.
We therefore obtain an industry- and size-matched control sample of firms with
potential goodwill impairment but which do not report an impairment loss in the
same quarter as the impairment firm. For each firm-quarter in the impairment
sample, we obtain a non-impairment control firm in the same year and quarter
matched on industry (2-digit SIC code), with size (market value) within a range of
±50%, and the closest book-to-market ratio as the impairment firm. Size and bookto-market ratio are measured at the beginning of the impairment quarter. The control
firms are required to have a non-zero balance in goodwill at the beginning of the
quarter and other required data on Compustat and CRSP. We require a close match
on the book-to-market ratio (a rough proxy for expected goodwill impairment) in
order to obtain a sample of control firms with similar expected impairment but zero
reported impairment.

Table 2 reports descriptive statistics for the impairment and control samples for
the full sample period as well as separately for the three reporting regimes—preSFAS-142, transition, and post-SFAS-142. From Panel A, the mean (median) aftertax impairment loss is $99 ($11) million; the significantly higher mean relative to
the median is consistent with a few very high magnitude losses–roughly 14% of
sample firms announce an impairment loss exceeding $100 million. The mean
(median) change in the announcement-quarter EPS of the impairment sample is
negative at -2.5% (-0.2%) and is significantly lower than that of the control
sample. For 622 impairment firms with data on I/B/E/S, the mean unexpected
earnings relative to the consensus forecast (scaled by price) is negative at -0.6%
compared with -0.1% for the control sample. Prior to the announcement, the
average firm in the impairment sample is significantly larger than the average
control firm but has comparable book-to-market ratio (by construction). The
difference in size is due to the shrinkage in the pool of candidate control firms after
matching on industry and the book-to-market ratio. Firms are evenly distributed
across industries, except for a higher concentration of firms in electronics (12.8%)
and business services (15.2%) groups (untabulated).

From Panel B, impairment loss is substantially higher in the transition period,
with the median loss being more than twice (three times) as high as that for the pre(post-) SFAS 142 period (significantly different at the 1% level). Twenty-three
percent of firms announce transition impairment losses in excess of $100 million;
the comparative numbers are 12 and 13% in the case of pre- and post-SFAS-142
impairment samples, respectively (untabulated). While the change in announcement-quarter EPS is negative on average for the pre- and post-SFAS-142
impairment samples, it is positive for the transition sample, suggesting that firms
that booked transition losses did not experience poor economic performance at that
time.

Variable definitions: Impairment loss is the goodwill impairment loss (net of tax) obtained from
announcements appearing in the Factiva database. Price-scaled impairment loss is the impairment loss
per share, scaled by Pt-2, the closing price on date t-2 relative to the loss announcement date t. EPS is
quarterly earnings per share before extraordinary items and discontinued operations for the fiscal quarter
immediately preceding the announcement date. Change in EPS is calculated relative to the same quarter
of the previous year and is scaled by Pt-2. Market value equals the closing price times the number of
common shares outstanding on date t-2. Book-to-Market ratio equals the per share book value of
common equity divided by price per share at the beginning of the announcement quarter. For the I/B/E/S
sample, unexpected earnings are calculated as actual EPS (reported on I/B/E/S) for the fiscal quarter
immediately preceding the announcement date minus the I/B/E/S mean consensus EPS forecast, where
the consensus is constructed over a period of 30 days preceding the earnings announcement date. The
control sample in Panel A is constructed by matching each impairment firm with a control firm, in the
same year and quarter, that belongs to the same industry (2-digit SIC code), with size within a ±50%
range, and the closest book-to-market ratio as the impairment firm
